pl-l3d34c4-d1e115.summary: Distinguishes four fears: worldly or human, servile, initial, and chaste, filial, or friendly.

pl-l3d34c4-d1e118.summary: Defines human fear, after Cassiodorus: fearing bodily danger or losing worldly goods, for which we sin. It is evil, abandoned with the world at the first step, and forbidden by the Lord: 'fear not those who kill the body'.
claims: Worldly fear is evil and leads to sin.

pl-l3d34c4-d1e127.summary: Defines servile fear, after Augustine: restraining oneself from sin through fear of hell, fearing the judge and penalties, doing good from fear of suffering evil, not of losing the eternal good, which one does not love; fearing hell, not the loss of the bridegroom's embrace. This fear is good and useful, though insufficient, and gradually forms a habit of justice.
claims: Servile fear fears penalty, not loss of the good.
Servile fear is good and useful but insufficient.
Servile fear gradually forms a habit of justice.

pl-l3d34c4-d1e134.summary: Describes initial fear, which follows when what was hard begins to be loved, and servile fear begins to be excluded by charity.
claims: Initial fear arises as charity begins to exclude servile fear.

pl-l3d34c4-d1e137.summary: Describes chaste or friendly fear, by which we fear lest the bridegroom delay or depart, lest we offend him or lose him. This fear comes from love; servile fear is useful but not everlasting, unlike this one. Divine fear accompanies every stage.
claims: Chaste fear comes from love and fears losing God.
Chaste fear is everlasting; servile fear is not.

pl-l3d34c4-d1e140.summary: Notes that four fears are distinguished here while Bede said two: Bede omitted human fear and included servile and initial under 'servile', calling friendly fear chaste.
claims: Bede's twofold division is reconciled with the fourfold one.

pl-l3d34c4-d1e149.summary: Adds that Augustine clearly distinguishes servile and chaste fear on Romans 8:15: one fear is in perfect charity, chaste fear; the other is not in charity, servile fear, in which one believes God but not in God, and does good but not well, since no one does well unwillingly.
claims: Chaste fear is in perfect charity; servile fear is outside charity.
In servile fear one does good but not well.

pl-l3d34c4.summary: Distinguishes four fears: worldly or human, servile, initial, and chaste or filial. Human fear, per Cassiodorus, fears bodily danger or loss of worldly goods and leads to sin; it is evil and abandoned at the first step. Servile fear, per Augustine, restrains from sin by fear of hell, not by love of the eternal good; it is good and useful, though insufficient, and builds a habit of justice. Initial fear follows when what was hard begins to be loved, and servile fear begins to be excluded. Chaste fear fears the bridegroom's absence or offending him, and comes from love. Bede's two fears include servile and initial under 'servile'; Augustine distinguishes servile fear, outside charity, from chaste fear, in perfect charity.
claims: There are four fears: worldly, servile, initial, and chaste.
Servile fear is good and useful but insufficient.
Initial fear begins when one starts to love what was hard.
Chaste fear comes from love and fears separation from God.
